flashcards.definition: A touch panel for pointer control; it can mean a laptop's built-in touchpad, but it often means a larger pad attached as a peripheral.
A large touch device attached as a peripheral, also called a graphics tablet, used mostly for sketching and painting in digital art apps; most work with a stylus.
A small pressure-sensitive nub built into the keyboard of some laptops that moves the cursor; the harder you press it, the faster the cursor moves.
A touch pen used instead of fingers on drawing pads and some touchscreens; it gives more precise control for handwriting and drawing, which is called natural input.
Records audio and is used for voice calls; on a laptop it sits behind a small hole in the top bezel next to the camera, with connections separate from the camera's.
Produce audio output; on a phone or tablet they are usually on the bottom edge, and more powerful external ones connect by the audio jack, USB/Lightning, or Bluetooth.
Used for video recording, web conferencing, and still pictures; a laptop's is typically built into the display assembly, so replacing it takes extensive disassembly.
Earbuds or headphones with a built-in microphone; wired ones use the 3.5 mm audio jack or a USB or Lightning connector, and wireless ones use Bluetooth.
A wired connection method: a modern laptop has a few Type A ports and one or more Type C ports, and phones and tablets use it for wired peripherals, charging, and tethering.
Attaches to a special connector on a laptop, or by USB, to add a full set of ports for a keyboard, monitor, mouse, and network, but normally adds no other functions.
A sophisticated port replicator that may also support add-in cards or drives in a media bay, so a docked laptop can work like a desktop.
The wireless radio in every laptop, smartphone, and tablet; a mobile device usually defaults to it when present, and turning cellular data off while leaving it on avoids data charges.
Usually two wires that run from the Wi-Fi chip around the edges of the display, in a laptop's lid, to pick up the strongest signal.
The cellular data generation just before 4G (LTE); each later generation, 4G and then 5G, is faster.
The cellular generation that introduced Long-Term Evolution (LTE) technology, with theoretical download speeds of up to 300 Mbps.
The cellular generation that builds on the earlier ones, with theoretical download speeds of up to 10 Gbps.
A small card that identifies the device on the mobile network; it is tied to the phone number and can usually be moved to a new phone.
A small chip inside the device that does a SIM card's job; it can be activated over the air, and many devices can store several profiles for different numbers or plans.
Connecting another device, such as a laptop, to a mobile device so it can share the mobile's cellular data connection, using a USB cable, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi.
Tethering over Wi-Fi: the mobile device is set up like an access point, with a network name, security type, and passphrase, for other devices to join.
Connecting two Bluetooth devices: enable Bluetooth, put both in discoverable mode, select the other device from the list of nearby devices, enter or confirm the PIN code, then test by using it.
The passkey the Bluetooth pairing system generates automatically when a connection request arrives; enter or confirm it on the destination device, then accept the connection.
Copying data such as contacts, calendar items, and mail back and forth between devices, or with a cloud service, so it stays up to date on each one.
A monthly limit on how much data a plan allows, with fees for going over; connect to Wi-Fi before syncing large files such as media.
Synced records with fields for name, address, email, and phone numbers.
Synced records of appointments or tasks, with fields such as subject, date, location, and participants.
Email as a synced business app: most systems keep messages on the server and each device manages them; choose IMAP to use one account on several devices.
Online storage that comes with the owner's account, such as iCloud or Google Drive; with permission, the device can back up to it, and a new device syncs from it.
A deployment model that lets employees use a personally owned device to access corporate accounts, apps, and data.
The part of an EMM suite that sets device policies for authentication, camera and microphone use, and connectivity, and can remotely wipe a device.
Authorized work apps, such as corporate email and calendar, that run in an enterprise workspace and keep their data apart from personal apps.
The service a device runs to find its position from GPS satellites or from nearby radio sources; an app can use it only with the user's permission.
Works out a device's latitude and longitude from information received from orbiting satellites; it needs a sensor that not every mobile device is fitted with.
Finding where a device is from how close it is to nearby cell towers, rather than from GPS satellites.
A removable, rechargeable lithium-ion (Li-ion) pack; turn the laptop off and unplug it before removing one.
A Mini PCIe or M.2 adapter that gives a laptop Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and/or cellular data; when replacing one, reconnect the antenna wires, and for a cellular adapter, insert the SIM card.
Almost always replaced with the same part, usually on a latched ribbon cable, and set to the correct input region; pry off one key cap with a flat blade.
A sensor that records a template of a body feature unique to the user; on a laptop, usually a fingerprint scanner, though the camera can scan a face or an iris.
A laptop's NFC sensor, used mainly to pair peripherals or connect to a smartphone; it may be part of the keyboard, touchpad, or fingerprint reader and must be connected to its antenna.
A battery that will not hold a charge has reached the end of its useful life; test with a known good battery, and if that fails too, suspect the motherboard's power circuitry.
Using an incorrect charger or cable risks fire or even explosion, and a poor charging routine shortens battery life; use the manufacturer's or an approved charger.
A bulging battery, seen as a device that wobbles when laid flat or a deformed touchpad or keyboard; stop using it at once, since it is a fire hazard.
Water under the screen, graphics artifacts, or no image; power off at once even with no visible sign, dry it fully, and usually replace the battery.
A connector that is loose or no longer fits, with no or intermittent data or poor charging; teach users to pull connectors straight out, never jiggling them.
Cracked or shattered glass, for example from a drop onto a hard surface; repair likely needs warranty or professional service.
A touch screen that ignores input or a stylus that stops working; check that the screen is clean and dry and the screen protector is flat, then restart the device.
A pointer that moves with no input or jumps while typing, which can happen if touchpad sensitivity is too high; update drivers, adjust input options, and recalibrate inaccurate touch where supported.
A mobile device that cannot join or keep a Wi-Fi or Bluetooth link; first check that airplane mode is off and that the radio is enabled.
Malicious or rogue apps on a device; on a phone, signs include heavy power drain, high resource use, slowdowns, hitting the data limit unexpectedly, and blocked app installs.
A mobile device that has grown slow to respond, which heavy background activity, such as malware, can cause.
A device that cannot add new apps, which can happen when malware blocks them or when free space runs out.
